study.title: Luke 23 The righteous doomed, the sinner forgiven, and the burial of Jesus
study.overview: Luke 23 presents Jesus" passion as a conflict between human injustice and God's purpose. The chapter shows forced political accusations against Jesus, repeated statements of innocence by Pilate, the rejection of the crowd, the mockery of Herod and the soldiers, the crucifixion between evildoers, the conversion of one of the condemned and, finally, death, burial and observance of the Sabbath by women. The text highlights that Jesus is executed as if he were guilty, but is recognized by all sides as innocent; at the same time, his death becomes the way to forgiveness, the hope of the Kingdom and obedient faithfulness of God even in the apparent defeat.

outline.title: Jesus before Pilate and Herod
outline.explanation: Religious leaders turn spiritual accusations into political accusations to obtain a Roman condemnation. Pilate examines Jesus and declares not to find blame on him, but sends him to Herod by knowing that Jesus was a Galilean. Herod waits for a sign, receives silence from Jesus, and ends up joining the mockery. The result is the rapprochement between Pilate and Herod, united by the same attitude of contempt before Jesus.

outline.title: The pressure of the crowd and the delivery of Jesus
outline.explanation: Pilate insists on the third time that Jesus does not deserve death and even proposes to punish him and release him, but the crowd demands Barabbas and crucifixion. The text shows the moral inversion: a murderous rebel is released, and the innocent is delivered. Pilate ends up yielding at the popular will, revealing weakness in the face of pressure and failure to protect a recognized innocent man.

outline.title: The way of the cross, crucifixion, and promise to the evildoer
outline.explanation: Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross behind Jesus, while women lament. Jesus calls them to weep for themselves, for he proclaims days of judgment upon Jerusalem. On the cross, Jesus is treated with mockery by leaders, soldiers, and one of the evildoers, but the other recognizes the divine justice over himself and the innocence of Jesus. Jesus" response to the request for mercy culminates in the immediate promise to be with him in paradise.

outline.title: Death, signs, burial and rest on the Sabbath
outline.explanation: Darkness covers the earth, the veil of the temple tears down, and Jesus gives the spirit to the Father. The centurion reacts by glorifying God and calling Jesus the righteous, as the crowds knock on the chest and the followers watch from afar. Joseph of Arimathea, a good and just man, asks the body, puts him in a new tomb and the women watch the place attentively. Then they prepare fragrant aromas and oils, but rest on the Sabbath according to the commandment.

study.context: The chapter takes place in Jerusalem in the Passover period, when the Roman presence sought to maintain order. The text mentions Pilate, Herod, the chief priests, the leaders, the people, Roman soldiers and the Jewish council, showing a scenario of religious and civil authorities acting together, albeit by different motivations. The interest in quickly burying the body before the Sabbath also reflects the proximity of the sacred day. The biblical text does not require more historical details than these.
study.theology: Luke 23 teaches that Jesus suffers as the innocent Messiah, rejected by leaders, multitudes, and political power, but approved by God. The repeated declaration of innocence by Pilate, the testimony of the centurion and the very word of Jesus reveal that his death is not accidental defeat, but a redeeming way. The forgiveness offered to the repentant evildoer shows that grace reaches those who recognize his guilt and turns to Christ with simple faith. The tear of the veil suggests, in evangelical reading, that the death of Jesus opens new access to God, without the text needing to detail all its meaning. The Sabbath guarded by women confirms, by contrast, the tension between the apparent interruption of hope and the persevering fidelity of the disciples.

scholarViews.insight: The leaders exchanged religious accusations for political accusations, because they wanted a Roman condemnation; the accusation of banning the tribute and declaring himself king was mostly false.
Pilate solemnly declares that he finds no guilt in Jesus and yet gives in to the pressure of the people; this exposes the injustice of the process and the weakness of the governor.
Women prepared aromas and oils to embalm the body, which shows that at that time they did not expect the resurrection on the third day.

questions: Why does Luke so often insist on the innocence of Jesus, even when everyone around treats him as guilty?
What does the attitude of the second evildoer teach about repentance, fear of God and faith in Jesus in the midst of guilt?
In what ways does the pressure of the crowd and the fear of Pilate appear today when people avoid doing what is correct?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to choose between the crowd and Christ. When public opinion, fear of losing position or convenience push to injustice, the text calls the disciple to remain with the innocent Jesus. It is also appropriate to imitate the women and Joseph of Arimathea: to observe carefully, to persevere in fidelity and to honor Christ even when hope seems silent. Finally, the prayer of the evildoer can become daily prayer: ask Jesus to remember us and trust that his mercy is sufficient.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail the meaning of the torn veil, nor do they allow to affirm with certainty all the theological developments of this sign beyond what the text suggests. Nor is it possible to specify, based only on the notes, whether the expression of paradise should be understood here in relation to the future resurrection or immediate communion with Christ; Tyndale's note only points to this possibility. Historical information was kept only where the notes support them.
